events.title: EMERGENCE OF HUMANS
events.description: Homo sapiens appear in Africa

details.title: Emergence of Humans
details.description: Homo sapiens appear in Africa
details.details: Fossil evidence suggests that Homo sapiens evolved in Africa around 300,000 years ago. The oldest known fossils were discovered in Jebel Irhoud, Morocco.
details.culturalContext: Early humans lived in small nomadic groups, using simple stone tools and developing early forms of communication.

events.title: EARLY HUMAN ART
events.description: Early evidence of symbolic thought and artistic expression

details.title: Early Human Art
details.description: Early evidence of symbolic thought and artistic expression
details.details: Blombos Cave in South Africa has engraved ochre and a cross-hatched ochre drawing about 73,000 years old, showing early humans making abstract designs. Ochre use and shell beads from African sites such as Bizmoune Cave in Morocco are older still, so symbolic behavior has a long, gradual history.
details.culturalContext: The development of symbolic thinking represents a major cognitive advancement in human evolution, possibly connected to language development.

events.title: OUT OF AFRICA
events.description: Main dispersal of modern humans from Africa, ancestral to all living non-Africans

details.title: OUT OF AFRICA
details.description: Main dispersal of modern humans from Africa, ancestral to all living non-Africans
details.details: The main dispersal that peopled Eurasia and Australia is usually placed roughly 70,000 to 50,000 years ago. Homo sapiens fossils in Africa go back to about 300,000 years (Jebel Irhoud), and earlier movements out of Africa, such as Misliya Cave in Israel (about 180,000 years) and Skhul and Qafzeh (about 120,000 to 90,000 years), left little trace in living people. Genetics shows non-Africans carry about 1 to 2 percent Neanderthal DNA from mixing after the exodus.
details.culturalContext: Early modern humans lived through repeated climate swings that opened and closed routes across the Sahara and Arabia. The dispersal spread them into environments already held by Neanderthals and Denisovans.

events.title: CULTURAL REVOLUTION
events.description: Period of advanced stone tool industries, cave art, and expanded social networks

details.title: CULTURAL REVOLUTION
details.description: Period of advanced stone tool industries, cave art, and expanded social networks
details.details: The Upper Paleolithic began in Europe about 45,000 to 50,000 years ago, with blade tools, worked bone and antler, and personal ornaments. Figurative art appears early: a painted pig in Sulawesi is dated to at least 45,000 years ago, and the Lion-Man ivory figure from Germany to about 40,000 years ago. Many researchers now see this as a gradual build-up rather than a sudden revolution.
details.culturalContext: Larger populations and long-distance exchange of shell and stone spread new ideas. Similar behaviors appear in Africa much earlier, so the label 'revolution' is debated.

events.title: CAVE PAINTINGS
events.description: Remarkable cave paintings appear in Europe, as at Chauvet in France

details.title: Cave Paintings
details.description: Remarkable cave paintings appear in Europe, as at Chauvet in France
details.details: The cave of Chauvet in France holds some of the oldest well-preserved paintings, made roughly 37,000 to 33,000 years ago (some researchers argue for a younger date). They show animals, hand stencils and abstract symbols. Caves such as Lascaux were painted many thousands of years later.
details.culturalContext: These paintings may have had ritual or spiritual significance, though their purpose is debated.

events.title: LAST GLACIAL MAXIMUM
events.description: Period of maximum extent of ice sheets, with sea levels 120 meters lower than present day

details.title: LAST GLACIAL MAXIMUM
details.description: Period of maximum extent of ice sheets, with sea levels 120 meters lower than present day
details.details: Ice sheets reached their greatest extent roughly 26,500 to 19,000 years ago, covering much of Canada, northern Europe and Patagonia. Global sea level fell about 120 meters, exposing land such as Beringia, the North Sea basin and the Sunda shelf. Humans in Europe withdrew to southern refuges such as Iberia and the Balkans.
details.culturalContext: Cold, dry and windy conditions shrank habitable land and pushed populations into refuges. Lower seas created land bridges that later helped people enter the Americas.

events.title: EUROPE
events.description: Flourishing of the Magdalenian culture in Western Europe, known for sophisticated bone/antler tools and renowned cave art (e.g., Lascaux, Altamira).

details.title: EUROPE
details.description: Flourishing of the Magdalenian culture in Western Europe, known for sophisticated bone/antler tools and renowned cave art (e.g., Lascaux, Altamira).
details.details: The Magdalenian is dated to roughly 17,000 to 12,000 years ago (about 15,000 to 10,000 BCE) and spread from Iberia to Poland. Its people made harpoons, barbed points and spear-throwers from antler, and eyed bone needles for tailored clothing. Lascaux in France and Altamira in Spain hold famous cave paintings of bison, horses and deer, with Altamira's Magdalenian phase dated to about 16,000 years ago.
details.culturalContext: Magdalenian groups were mobile reindeer and horse hunters who traded shells and flint over long distances. Cave art and decorated portable objects point to shared symbolic traditions across Western Europe.

events.title: NORTHERN HEMISPHERE CLIMATE
events.description: A significant warming period begins after the Last Glacial Maximum, leading to ice sheet retreat and ecosystem changes.

details.title: Northern Hemisphere Climate
details.description: A significant warming period begins after the Last Glacial Maximum, leading to ice sheet retreat and ecosystem changes.
details.details: The Bølling-Allerød interstadial lasted from about 14,700 to 12,900 years ago. Greenland ice cores show a warming of several degrees within decades, and meltwater pulse 1A raised sea level by many meters in a few centuries. Forests spread north, and glaciers retreated across Europe and North America.
details.culturalContext: Warmer conditions let hunter-gatherers recolonize northern Europe and supported larger, more settled groups such as the Natufians in the Near East.

events.title: NORTHERN HEMISPHERE CLIMATE
events.description: An abrupt return to near-glacial conditions interrupts the post-glacial warming trend, lasting over a millennium.

details.title: Northern Hemisphere Climate
details.description: An abrupt return to near-glacial conditions interrupts the post-glacial warming trend, lasting over a millennium.
details.details: The Younger Dryas was a return to cold conditions from about 12,900 to 11,700 years ago, named after the Arctic flower Dryas octopetala found in European sediments. It is best documented around the North Atlantic. The leading explanation is that meltwater from North American ice sheets weakened the Atlantic circulation that carries warmth north.
details.culturalContext: Cooler, drier conditions in the Near East stressed wild food supplies. Some researchers link this to more intensive plant use among the Natufians, though that link is debated.

events.title: NORTH AMERICA [THEORETICAL]
events.description: Hypothesized comet/asteroid impact or airburst event proposed as a trigger for the Younger Dryas cooling and associated environmental changes.

details.title: NORTH AMERICA [THEORETICAL]
details.description: Hypothesized comet/asteroid impact or airburst event proposed as a trigger for the Younger Dryas cooling and associated environmental changes.
details.details: In 2007 Richard Firestone, Allen West, James Kennett and colleagues proposed that fragments of a comet exploded over North America about 12,800 years ago. They point to a thin layer at sites in North America, Europe and the Middle East holding nanodiamonds, metallic spherules, melted glass, platinum spikes and soot from widespread fires, all at the moment the Younger Dryas cold began.
details.culturalContext: If it happened, one event would explain the sudden return of the cold, the loss of mammoths and other giant animals, and the end of the Clovis culture. Some researchers link it to the world's fire and flood myths and to carvings at Göbekli Tepe such as the Vulture Stone. Many scientists dispute it, pointing to the lack of a crater, so the debate is still open.

events.title: NORTH AMERICA
events.description: Accelerated extinction of large mammals (mammoths, mastodons) and significant transformation/decline of the Clovis Paleo-Indian culture coincides with Younger Dryas onset.

details.title: NORTH AMERICA
details.description: Accelerated extinction of large mammals (mammoths, mastodons) and significant transformation/decline of the Clovis Paleo-Indian culture coincides with Younger Dryas onset.
details.details: About 35 genera of large North American mammals, including mammoths, mastodons, giant ground sloths and camels, vanished roughly 13,000 to 11,000 years ago. The Clovis tradition, known for fluted spear points, lasted only a few centuries around 13,000 years ago before giving way to regional point types such as Folsom. Sites like Blackwater Draw and Murray Springs show Clovis hunters killing mammoth.
details.culturalContext: The cause is debated. Most scholars favor a mix of rapid climate change and human hunting, with some weight on habitat loss. Pre-Clovis sites such as Monte Verde and White Sands show people arrived earlier than Clovis.

events.title: NORTHERN HEMISPHERE CLIMATE
events.description: Rapid warming resumes, marking the end of the last major cold period of the Pleistocene and the beginning of the Holocene epoch.

details.title: Northern Hemisphere Climate
details.description: Rapid warming resumes, marking the end of the last major cold period of the Pleistocene and the beginning of the Holocene epoch.
details.details: The Younger Dryas ended about 11,700 years ago, with Greenland ice cores showing warming of several degrees in a few decades. That date also marks the formal start of the Holocene epoch. Ice sheets kept shrinking and sea level rose, setting conditions for the spread of farming in the Near East.
details.culturalContext: Warmer, wetter, more stable conditions favored plant cultivation and settled life. The first monumental sites and villages in the Near East followed soon after.

events.shortDesc: Often called the world's oldest temple
events.title: GÖBEKLI TEPE
events.description: Construction of massive stone pillars arranged in circles with carved animals and symbols in modern-day Turkey

details.shortDesc: Often called the world's oldest temple
details.title: Göbekli Tepe
details.description: Construction of massive stone pillars arranged in circles with carved animals and symbols in modern-day Turkey
details.details: Göbekli Tepe consists of massive stone pillars arranged in circles, many decorated with carvings of animals and abstract symbols. The site predates pottery, metallurgy, writing, and even farming.
details.culturalContext: The construction of Göbekli Tepe suggests complex social organization and religious practices before the development of agriculture, challenging previous theories about the development of civilization.

events.title: EARLY CULTIVATION
events.description: Early evidence of intentional plant management and farming techniques developing across fertile regions

details.title: EARLY CULTIVATION
details.description: Early evidence of intentional plant management and farming techniques developing across fertile regions
details.details: Wild cereals were gathered and ground at Ohalo II in Israel as early as about 23,000 years ago. By roughly 9500 BCE communities in the Levant and Anatolia were tending wild cereals and pulses, and clearly domesticated emmer, einkorn, barley, lentils and peas appear by about 8500 to 8000 BCE. Domestication was gradual and took place in several places.
details.culturalContext: Cultivation grew from foraging economies in the Fertile Crescent after the climate warmed. It tied people to fields and storage and eventually supported larger villages.
artifacts: Tell Aswad and Jericho plant remains

events.title: FERTILE CRESCENT
events.description: Early farming villages in the Middle East cultivate wild and early forms of grains like wheat and barley

details.title: Fertile Crescent
details.description: Villages in the Fertile Crescent cultivated wild and early forms of grains like wheat and barley. Goats and sheep were domesticated there soon after, leading to the first settled agricultural communities.
details.details: Early farmers in the Fertile Crescent began cultivating wild grains like wheat and barley, and domesticating animals such as goats and sheep, leading to the first settled agricultural communities.
details.culturalContext: The shift to agriculture fundamentally changed human society, allowing for permanent settlements, population growth, food surpluses, and eventually social stratification.

events.title: JERICHO
events.description: Development of one of the world's oldest settlements, with a stone wall and tower

details.title: Jericho
details.description: Development of one of the world's oldest settlements, with a stone wall and tower
details.details: Archaeological evidence shows that Jericho (Tell es-Sultan) had a large stone wall and a stone tower by about 8300 BCE, among the earliest examples of monumental architecture. Their purpose is debated, with defense, flood control and ritual or astronomical uses all proposed.
details.culturalContext: The wall and tower suggest organized communal labor on a scale previously unseen, and possibly emerging social complexity.

events.title: NEAR EAST
events.description: Domestication of cattle, kept at first mainly for meat and hides, in the Near East region

details.title: NEAR EAST
details.description: Domestication of cattle, kept at first mainly for meat and hides, in the Near East region
details.details: By 8000 BCE, there is clear evidence of morphological changes indicating cattle domestication. These animals provided reliable meat and hides. Milk use is attested from about 6500 BCE, and pulling and plowing came later.
details.culturalContext: Animal domestication created a more secure food supply and provided new resources, fundamentally altering human relationships with the environment.

events.title: ANATOLIA
events.description: The monumental structures at Göbekli Tepe are intentionally buried under layers of earth, preserving the site.

details.title: ANATOLIA
details.description: The monumental structures at Göbekli Tepe are intentionally buried under layers of earth, preserving the site.
details.details: By about 8000 BCE Göbekli Tepe's stone enclosures were filled with soil, flint, tools and animal bones. Klaus Schmidt, who excavated the site, saw this as a deliberate burial at the end of its use. Some later excavators argue that slope erosion and collapse did part of the work.
details.culturalContext: Whether the site was ritually closed or simply abandoned and slowly covered is unresolved. Either way, building at Göbekli Tepe stopped as farming villages in the region grew.

events.title: SOUTHWEST ASIA
events.description: Evidence of early domestication of sheep, goats, and other animals for food and materials

details.title: Southwest Asia
details.description: Evidence of early domestication of sheep, goats, and other animals for food and materials
details.details: By 8000 BCE, there is clear evidence of morphological changes in sheep and goats indicating domestication. These animals provided reliable meat and hides. Milk came into use within a few thousand years, and wool sheep appeared later, around the 4th millennium BCE.
details.culturalContext: Animal domestication created a more secure food supply and provided new resources for clothing and tools, fundamentally altering human relationships with the environment.

events.title: SOUTH ASIA
events.description: Early agricultural settlement in the Indus Valley region, precursor to the Indus Valley Civilization

details.title: SOUTH ASIA
details.description: Early agricultural settlement in the Indus Valley region, precursor to the Indus Valley Civilization
details.details: Mehrgarh lies on the Kachi Plain in Balochistan, Pakistan, and was occupied from about 7000 BCE into the Bronze Age. Early residents built mudbrick houses, grew wheat and barley, and kept cattle, sheep and goats. Burials include early evidence of drilled teeth, and the site shows continuous change toward the later Indus cities.
details.culturalContext: Mehrgarh shows farming arriving in South Asia, probably through contact with the Near East and local domestication of cattle. Its crafts and settlement layout have links to the Indus Valley Civilization that arose about 2600 BCE.

events.title: ÇATALHÖYÜK
events.description: Large Neolithic settlement in Anatolia with houses built adjacent to each other and entered through roofs

details.title: Çatalhöyük
details.description: Large Neolithic settlement in Anatolia with houses built adjacent to each other and entered through roofs
details.details: Çatalhöyük was a large Neolithic settlement in southern Anatolia, with houses built directly adjacent to each other with no streets or pathways between them. Residents entered their homes through holes in the roof.
details.culturalContext: The site provides insights into early urban living, with evidence of complex religious practices, art, and craft specialization.

events.title: CHINA
events.description: Early symbolic markings found on tortoise shells and bone in Jiahu, China, possibly representing an early form of proto-writing

details.title: CHINA
details.description: Early symbolic markings found on tortoise shells and bone in Jiahu, China, possibly representing an early form of proto-writing
details.details: Jiahu in Henan Province was occupied from about 7000 to 5700 BCE. Archaeologists found around a dozen carved symbols on tortoise shells, bone and pottery, dated to about 6600 BCE. Most scholars do not call them writing, since they are too few and no link to later Chinese script is established.
details.culturalContext: Jiahu villagers grew rice, made fermented drinks and played flutes made from crane bones. The symbols may have had ritual or marking purposes.

events.title: POTTERY INNOVATION
events.description: Widespread adoption of fired pottery for storage, cooking, and artistic expression across the Near East

details.title: Pottery Innovation
details.description: Widespread adoption of fired pottery for storage, cooking, and artistic expression across the Near East
details.details: Pottery was first made in East Asia more than 15,000 years ago and came into wide use in the Near East by about 6500 BCE. It allowed better food storage and new cooking methods. Early pottery was often decorated with geometric patterns and later with representations of animals and humans.
details.culturalContext: Pottery production represents an important technological advancement that facilitated the storage of agricultural surpluses and the cooking of new types of food.

events.title: EUROPEAN EXPANSION
events.description: Agricultural techniques and domesticated crops spread into Europe through the Balkans and along the Mediterranean

details.title: European Expansion
details.description: Agricultural techniques and domesticated crops spread into Europe through the Balkans and along the Mediterranean
details.details: The Neolithic way of life spread into Europe from Anatolia and the Near East, bringing domesticated plants, animals, and the knowledge of pottery making and settled agriculture.
details.culturalContext: The spread of agriculture into Europe represents one of the most significant demographic and cultural transformations in human history, eventually replacing hunting and gathering as the dominant lifestyle.

events.title: GROWING SETTLEMENTS
events.description: Larger settlements show specialized crafts, trade, and early signs of social differences

details.title: Growing Settlements
details.description: Larger settlements show specialized crafts, trade, and early signs of social differences
details.details: As settlements grew in size and complexity, evidence emerges of specialized craft production, trade networks, and early signs of social difference, such as variations in burial goods and housing quality.
details.culturalContext: These early forms of social complexity laid the groundwork for the subsequent development of more formalized hierarchies and eventually state-level societies in the following millennia.

events.title: EUROPE
events.description: Advanced Neolithic culture in Southeast Europe known for sophisticated pottery and early copper metallurgy

details.title: EUROPE
details.description: Advanced Neolithic culture in Southeast Europe known for sophisticated pottery and early copper metallurgy
details.details: The Vinča culture flourished in Serbia and neighboring countries from about 5400 to 4500 BCE, centered on Vinča-Belo Brdo near Belgrade. It is known for burnished pottery, large settlements with multi-room houses and many clay figurines. Copper slag at Belovode and Pločnik shows copper smelting from about 5000 BCE.
details.culturalContext: Vinča communities were among the largest in Neolithic Europe. Their incised Vinča signs resemble writing but are generally not regarded as a true script.

events.title: COPPER WORKING
events.description: Earliest secure evidence of copper smelting, in the Balkans, after thousands of years of hammering native copper

details.title: Copper Working
details.description: Earliest secure evidence of copper smelting, in the Balkans, after thousands of years of hammering native copper
details.details: Copper smelting, as opposed to hammering native copper, appears in the Balkans by about 5000 BCE at sites such as Belovode and Pločnik in Serbia. Hammered native copper beads and pins are known from Anatolia several thousand years earlier. Smelting is also known from Iran and Anatolia in the fifth millennium BCE.
details.culturalContext: Smelting may have grown out of potters' skill with hot kilns, and copper tools and ornaments soon marked wealth and status.
artifacts: Varna gold and copper grave goods

events.title: MESOPOTAMIA
events.description: Development of sophisticated irrigation systems in Mesopotamia, enabling large-scale agriculture in arid regions

details.title: Mesopotamia
details.description: Development of irrigation in the Tigris-Euphrates valley
details.details: Early Mesopotamians developed sophisticated irrigation systems, digging canals to bring water from rivers to fields, allowing for intensive agriculture in an otherwise arid region.
details.culturalContext: Control of water resources became central to political power in early Mesopotamia, with irrigation projects requiring coordinated labor and centralized authority.

events.title: TRADE NETWORKS
events.description: Extensive trade networks develop across the Near East, exchanging raw materials, finished goods, and ideas

details.title: Trade Networks
details.description: Extensive trade networks develop across the Near East, exchanging raw materials, finished goods, and ideas
details.details: By the Ubaid period, roughly 6500 to 3800 BCE, goods moved over long distances in the Near East. Anatolian obsidian, Gulf shell, and Iranian stone reached Mesopotamian villages, and Ubaid-style pottery spread along the Persian Gulf and into Syria.
details.culturalContext: Southern Mesopotamia lacked stone, metal and timber, so its communities depended on exchange with the highlands around them.

events.title: FIRST SUMERIAN CITIES
events.description: Rise of the first true cities in southern Mesopotamia, with Uruk becoming the world's largest urban center

details.title: First Sumerian Cities
details.description: Rise of the first true cities in southern Mesopotamia, with Uruk becoming the world's largest urban center
details.details: Uruk, in southern Mesopotamia, grew through the Uruk period (about 4000 to 3100 BCE). By about 3200 BCE it covered roughly 250 hectares and held monumental temple precincts such as Eanna, making it the largest known city of its time.
details.culturalContext: Irrigation farming, temple economies and craft specialization let large populations gather and be managed in one place.

events.title: ADMINISTRATIVE TOKENS
events.description: Development of clay tokens, seals, and counting devices for record keeping in Mesopotamia

details.title: Administrative Tokens
details.description: Development of clay tokens, seals, and counting devices for record keeping in Mesopotamia
details.details: Small clay tokens in set shapes were used in the Near East from about 8000 BCE to track goods such as grain and livestock. By the later fourth millennium BCE they were sealed in clay envelopes and impressed with cylinder seals. Some scholars see this as a step toward writing, but that link is debated.
details.culturalContext: Record keeping grew out of temple and household accounting, as larger economies needed a way to track goods and debts.

events.title: WHEEL TECHNOLOGY
events.description: Wheels come into use for pottery making and for carts and wagons, appearing in Mesopotamia and Europe by about 3500 BCE

details.title: Wheel Technology
details.description: Wheel technology transforms transportation and pottery production
details.details: Turntables for shaping pots were used in the Near East before wheeled vehicles. The earliest evidence of wheeled vehicles dates to about 3500 BCE and appears at about the same time in Mesopotamia, the Northern Caucasus and Central Europe, so where the wheel was first invented is unknown. Early wheels were solid wooden discs attached to axles.
details.culturalContext: The wheel revolutionized transportation, trade, and warfare, allowing for the movement of heavier loads over longer distances and contributing to the expansion of early states.

events.title: PREDYNASTIC DEVELOPMENTS
events.description: Formation of early Egyptian states in the Nile Valley prior to unification

details.title: Predynastic Developments
details.description: Formation of early Egyptian states in the Nile Valley prior to unification
details.details: In the Predynastic period (about 4500 to 3100 BCE) Egyptian farming cultures grew along the Nile. Naqada culture spread from Upper Egypt, with rich elite burials at Hierakonpolis and Abydos, and regional rulers emerged before unification.
details.culturalContext: The Nile floods gave reliable harvests, and control of trade and farmland let local chiefs become kings.

events.title: SUMERIAN CUNEIFORM
events.description: Development of cuneiform writing in Mesopotamia, one of the world's earliest writing systems

details.title: Sumerian Cuneiform
details.description: Development of writing in Sumer (cuneiform) revolutionizes record keeping
details.details: Cuneiform began as pictographs drawn on clay tablets with a pointed reed stylus, primarily for recording economic transactions. Over time the signs became wedge-shaped and abstract, and the system could express complex ideas and narratives.
details.culturalContext: Writing allowed for more complex administration, the preservation of knowledge, literature, and religious texts, fundamentally transforming how societies functioned and remembered their past.

events.title: NARMER'S CONQUEST
events.description: Unification of Upper and Lower Egypt under King Narmer, traditionally founding the First Dynasty

details.title: Narmer's Conquest
details.description: Unification of Upper and Lower Egypt under King Narmer, traditionally founding the First Dynasty
details.details: Around 3100 BCE, Egypt was unified under a single king, traditionally founding the First Dynasty. Narmer is the best-documented ruler of this moment, shown wearing the crowns of both lands on his palette. Whether he is the later tradition's Menes is debated.
details.culturalContext: Later Egyptians remembered unification as the start of their kingdom, and the double crown became a lasting symbol of kingship.

events.title: URBAN CENTERS
events.description: Development of major city-states like Ur, Uruk, and Lagash in Mesopotamia

details.title: Urban Centers
details.description: Development of major city-states like Ur, Uruk, and Lagash in Mesopotamia
details.details: In the Early Dynastic period, roughly 2900 to 2350 BCE, southern Mesopotamia held rival city-states such as Ur, Uruk, Lagash, Umma and Kish. Each had its own ruler, patron god and temple, and they fought over canals and borders.
details.culturalContext: City-states shared language and religion but competed politically, and kings claimed to rule on behalf of the city's god.

events.title: PYRAMID AGE
events.description: Beginning of the Old Kingdom period in Egypt, known for monumental architecture including the Step Pyramid and Great Pyramids

details.title: Pyramid Age
details.description: Beginning of the Old Kingdom, the Pyramid Age, with the Step Pyramid at Saqqara
details.details: The Old Kingdom began around 2700 BCE, and King Djoser's Step Pyramid at Saqqara, designed by Imhotep, was the first large stone pyramid. The Great Pyramid of Giza, built later for Pharaoh Khufu, was the tallest human-made structure in the world for over 3,800 years. The pyramids demonstrate the extraordinary organizational capacity and engineering skills of ancient Egyptians.
details.culturalContext: The pyramids were part of elaborate funerary complexes designed to ensure the pharaoh's successful journey to the afterlife, reflecting Egyptian religious beliefs about death and immortality.

events.title: KHUFU'S MONUMENT
events.description: Construction of the Great Pyramid of Giza, the largest of the Egyptian pyramids and one of the Seven Wonders of the Ancient World

details.title: Khufu's Monument
details.description: Construction of the Great Pyramid of Giza, the largest of the Egyptian pyramids and one of the Seven Wonders of the Ancient World
details.details: The Great Pyramid at Giza was built for Pharaoh Khufu of the Fourth Dynasty, who reigned about 2589 to 2566 BCE. It originally stood about 146 meters tall and was the tallest human-made structure for many centuries. It is the only one of the Seven Wonders still standing.
details.culturalContext: Pyramids tied the king's afterlife to the order of the state, and building them drew labor and supplies from across Egypt.

events.title: HARAPPAN CULTURE
events.description: Urban civilization in South Asia with sophisticated city planning, drainage systems, and standardized weights and measures

details.title: Harappan Culture
details.description: Advanced urban centers at Mohenjo-daro and Harappa flourish
details.details: The Indus Valley Civilization featured remarkably well-planned cities with grid layouts, sophisticated drainage systems, standardized weights and measures, and a still-undeciphered writing system.
details.culturalContext: Despite its sophistication, much about Harappan society remains mysterious, including its governance structure, religious practices, and the reasons for its eventual decline.

events.title: SARGON'S CONQUEST
events.description: Sargon of Akkad creates one of the world's earliest empires, uniting Mesopotamia under a single ruler

details.title: Sargon's Conquest
details.description: Sargon of Akkad creates one of the world's earliest empires, uniting Mesopotamia under a single ruler
details.details: By tradition Sargon of Akkad rose from cupbearer to king, and he ruled about 2334 to 2279 BCE by the usual dating. He conquered the Sumerian city-states and founded Akkad as his capital. His empire reached from the Persian Gulf toward the Mediterranean, and Akkadian became a written language of government.
details.culturalContext: Akkadians and Sumerians were distinct peoples, and the empire joined them under one royal house.
artifacts: Bronze head of an Akkadian ruler

events.title: SUMERIAN LITERATURE
events.description: Sumerian poems about Gilgamesh, king of Uruk, are composed and later joined into an epic of his quest for immortality

details.title: Sumerian Literature
details.description: Sumerian poems about Gilgamesh, king of Uruk, are composed and later joined into an epic of his quest for immortality
details.details: The Sumerians wrote poems about Gilgamesh, king of Uruk, by about 2100 BCE, and later scribes joined them into the Akkadian Epic of Gilgamesh. The story follows his grief at the death of Enkidu and his failed search for immortality. Gilgamesh was probably a real ruler of about 2600 BCE.
details.culturalContext: Literature of this kind was copied in scribal schools for centuries and shaped later Babylonian and Near Eastern storytelling.

events.title: CRETE
events.description: First advanced European civilization develops on Crete

details.title: Crete
details.description: First advanced European civilization develops on Crete
details.details: The Minoans built elaborate palace complexes, most famously at Knossos, developed a writing system (Linear A), and created sophisticated art and architecture. They were a major maritime trading power in the Mediterranean.
details.culturalContext: Minoan culture appears to have emphasized female deities, bull imagery, and maritime trade. Older claims that Minoan society was unusually peaceful are now doubted, since fortifications and weapons have been found.

periods.title: IRON AGE & CLASSICAL PERIOD (1,200 BCE - 500 CE)

events.title: WRITING INNOVATION
events.description: Development of the first widely used consonantal alphabet, ancestor of many modern scripts

details.title: Writing Innovation
details.description: Development of the first widely used consonantal alphabet, ancestor of many modern scripts
details.details: The Phoenician alphabet of about 22 letters, used by Canaanite cities such as Byblos and Tyre, is conventionally dated to about 1050 BCE. It wrote consonants only. Greeks adapted it by about 800 BCE by adding vowels, and the Latin and Cyrillic scripts descend from that Greek form.
details.culturalContext: Its small symbol set was far easier to learn than cuneiform or hieroglyphs, and Phoenician merchants carried it around the Mediterranean.

events.title: MARITIME TRADE
events.description: Phoenicians expand Mediterranean trade networks

details.title: Maritime Trade
details.description: Phoenicians expand Mediterranean trade networks
details.details: The Phoenicians established a network of colonies and trading posts throughout the Mediterranean, spreading their alphabet (the basis for many modern writing systems) and connecting diverse cultures through commerce.
details.culturalContext: As skilled seafarers and merchants, the Phoenicians facilitated cultural exchange between Egypt, Mesopotamia, and the emerging societies of Europe.

events.title: ROMAN BEGINNINGS
events.description: Traditional date for the founding of Rome

details.title: Roman Beginnings
details.description: Traditional date for the founding of Rome
details.details: According to legend, Rome was founded by Romulus, who with his twin brother Remus was raised by a she-wolf. Archaeological evidence shows early settlements on the Palatine Hill dating to this approximate period.
details.culturalContext: The founding myths of Rome were important to Roman identity and were elaborated over centuries to connect Rome with divine origins and destiny.

events.title: GOLDEN AGE OF GREECE
events.description: Advances in philosophy, art, and science in Athens

details.title: Golden Age of Greece
details.description: Advances in philosophy, art, and science in Athens
details.details: The Classical period in Athens saw the development of democracy under Pericles, the philosophical work of Socrates, Plato, and Aristotle, and architectural marvels like the Parthenon.
details.culturalContext: Athenian democracy, though limited to adult male citizens, represented a revolutionary political system that has influenced governments throughout history.

events.title: QIN DYNASTY
events.description: Qin Shi Huang unifies China and links older border walls into one defense

details.title: Qin Dynasty
details.description: Qin Shi Huang unifies China and links older border walls into one defense
details.details: Qin Shi Huang conquered the warring states of China, standardized weights, measures, and writing, built road networks, and joined and extended earlier northern walls to defend against invaders.
details.culturalContext: The Qin Dynasty established the centralized imperial system that would govern China for over two millennia, though the harsh Legalist policies of Qin Shi Huang led to the dynasty's quick collapse after his death.

events.title: AUGUSTUS
events.description: Roman Republic transitions to the Roman Empire

details.title: Augustus
details.description: Roman Republic transitions to the Roman Empire
details.details: After defeating Mark Antony and Cleopatra, Octavian became Augustus, the first Roman Emperor, establishing the Pax Romana (Roman Peace), a period of relative stability that lasted about 200 years.
details.culturalContext: Augustus maintained the facade of republican government while centralizing power, creating a model of imperial rule that balanced military power, legal authority, and public approval.

events.title: END OF WESTERN ROMAN EMPIRE
events.description: Romulus Augustulus is deposed, marking the fall of the Western Roman Empire

details.title: End of Western Roman Empire
details.description: Romulus Augustulus is deposed, marking the fall of the Western Roman Empire
details.details: The Germanic commander Odoacer deposed the last Western Roman Emperor, Romulus Augustulus, sending the imperial regalia to the Eastern Emperor Zeno and ruling Italy as a king rather than an emperor.
details.culturalContext: While traditionally seen as the 'fall' of Rome, this event was part of a gradual transformation rather than a sudden collapse, with many Roman institutions continuing under Germanic rule.

events.title: RISE OF ISLAM
events.description: Beginning of Islamic expansion across the Middle East and North Africa

details.title: Rise of Islam
details.description: Beginning of Islamic expansion across the Middle East and North Africa
details.details: Muhammad died in 632 CE after uniting much of Arabia. The caliphs who followed conquered Syria, Egypt and Iraq within about twenty years and toppled the Sasanian Empire by 651. The Umayyad caliphate later reached from Spain to Central Asia.
details.culturalContext: The conquests brought a new faith, the Arabic language and a shared system of law to a large area of older civilizations.

events.title: CHARLEMAGNE
events.description: Charlemagne crowned emperor in Rome by Pope Leo III

details.title: Charlemagne
details.description: Charlemagne crowned emperor in Rome by Pope Leo III
details.details: On Christmas Day 800 CE, Pope Leo III crowned Charlemagne emperor in Rome. As King of the Franks since 768, he had united much of western Europe. His court at Aachen supported the Carolingian Renaissance in schools and manuscripts. The Holy Roman Empire is usually dated from Otto I in 962, though some trace it back to this coronation.
details.culturalContext: The coronation revived the idea of a Roman empire in the West and tied the Frankish kings to the papacy.

events.title: SOUTHEAST ASIAN POWER
events.description: Angkor Empire reaches its peak in Southeast Asia

details.title: Southeast Asian Power
details.description: Angkor Empire reaches its peak in Southeast Asia
details.details: The Khmer Empire, centered at Angkor in Cambodia, was strong from the ninth to fifteenth century. Under Jayavarman VII, who reigned from about 1181 to about 1218, it reached its widest extent and built Angkor Thom and the Bayon. Suryavarman II had built Angkor Wat earlier, in the early 1100s.
details.culturalContext: Khmer kings used Hindu and then Buddhist ideas of kingship, and a huge network of reservoirs and canals fed the capital.

events.title: COLUMBUS
events.description: Columbus reaches the Americas, beginning sustained European colonization

details.title: Columbus
details.description: Columbus reaches the Americas, beginning sustained European colonization
details.details: Christopher Columbus sailed from Palos, Spain, in August 1492 with three ships under the backing of Spain's Catholic Monarchs. He landed in the Bahamas on 12 October 1492 and later reached Cuba and Hispaniola. Three further voyages followed before 1504.
details.culturalContext: The voyages opened sustained contact between Europe and the Americas, which brought the Columbian Exchange of crops, animals and diseases. Indigenous peoples of the Americas experienced severe population loss and the start of sustained European colonization.
artifacts: Las Casas's abstract of Columbus's log

events.title: MODERN SCIENCE
events.description: Scientific method and empirical research transform knowledge

details.title: Modern Science
details.description: Scientific method and empirical research transform knowledge
details.details: Between roughly 1543 and 1687, works such as Copernicus's On the Revolutions, Galileo's telescope observations (1610) and Newton's Principia (1687) changed how nature was studied. Francis Bacon argued for systematic experiment, and the Royal Society was founded in London in 1660.
details.culturalContext: Observation, measurement and mathematics came to be treated as the basis for understanding nature. Scientific societies and printed journals let results be shared and checked across Europe.
artifacts: On the Revolutions of the Heavenly Spheres

events.title: NAPOLEON
events.description: Napoleon Bonaparte crowned Emperor of France

details.title: Napoleon
details.description: Napoleon Bonaparte crowned Emperor of France
details.details: Napoleon Bonaparte took power in France in 1799 and was crowned Emperor at Notre-Dame in Paris on 2 December 1804. The Napoleonic Code of 1804 standardized French civil law. His wars reshaped Europe until his defeat at Waterloo in 1815.
details.culturalContext: Napoleon's rule consolidated many changes of the French Revolution, including legal equality and a centralized state. The Napoleonic Code influenced legal systems across Europe and in Latin America.
artifacts: Coronation of Napoleon (painting by Jacques-Louis David)

events.title: GLOBAL CONFLICT
events.description: First worldwide industrial war begins

details.title: Global Conflict
details.description: First worldwide industrial war begins
details.details: The war began in July 1914 after the assassination of Archduke Franz Ferdinand of Austria-Hungary in Sarajevo on 28 June. The Allied Powers and Central Powers fought mainly on the Western and Eastern Fronts until the armistice of 11 November 1918. An estimated 9 to 10 million soldiers died.
details.culturalContext: Machine guns, artillery, poison gas, aircraft and tanks made it an industrial war. Its end brought the collapse of four empires, the Treaty of Versailles in 1919 and the League of Nations.

events.title: MODERN WORLD
events.description: Soviet Union dissolves, ending the Cold War

details.title: Modern World
details.description: Soviet Union dissolves, ending the Cold War
details.details: The Soviet Union was formally dissolved on 26 December 1991, after Soviet republics declared independence and 15 successor states emerged. The Berlin Wall had opened in November 1989 and Germany reunified in October 1990. Russia took the Soviet seat at the United Nations.
details.culturalContext: The Soviet and American blocs had been in rivalry since the late 1940s. The end of the Soviet Union ended that division and led to new states in Eastern Europe and Central Asia, and to later NATO and EU enlargement.

events.title: WAR ON TERROR
events.description: Terrorist attacks in the United States lead to global conflicts and security changes

details.title: War on Terror
details.description: Terrorist attacks in the United States lead to global conflicts and security changes
details.details: On 11 September 2001, hijackers flew two airliners into the World Trade Center in New York and one into the Pentagon, and a fourth crashed in Pennsylvania. Nearly 3,000 people died. The United States led an invasion of Afghanistan in October 2001, and a 2003 invasion of Iraq followed.
details.culturalContext: The attacks led to new security measures such as the creation of the US Department of Homeland Security and the USA PATRIOT Act. Military operations in Afghanistan and Iraq lasted many years and are still debated.

events.title: ECONOMIC RECESSION
events.description: Worldwide economic downturn triggered by the collapse of the housing market

details.title: Economic Recession
details.description: Worldwide economic downturn triggered by the collapse of the housing market
details.details: The crisis followed a fall in US house prices and growing defaults on subprime mortgages. Lehman Brothers filed for bankruptcy on 15 September 2008. Governments and central banks responded with bailouts, interest rate cuts and stimulus, and many countries entered recession.
details.culturalContext: It was the most severe global downturn since the Great Depression of the 1930s. It led to new bank regulation, such as the US Dodd-Frank Act of 2010 and the Basel III standards, and to a long debate over austerity and stimulus.

events.title: MIDDLE EAST REVOLUTIONS
events.description: Wave of pro-democracy protests and uprisings across the Arab world

details.title: Middle East Revolutions
details.description: Wave of pro-democracy protests and uprisings across the Arab world
details.details: The protests began in Tunisia in December 2010 and spread in 2011 to Egypt, Libya, Yemen, Bahrain and Syria. The Tunisian and Egyptian presidents left office early in 2011. Outcomes varied widely, including political change, civil wars in Libya, Syria and Yemen, and continued rule elsewhere.
details.culturalContext: Protesters raised demands about political freedoms, living costs and unemployment. Social media and satellite television helped spread information, and the consequences are still debated across the region.

events.title: COVID-19
events.description: Worldwide health crisis that transformed global society and economies

details.title: COVID-19
details.description: Worldwide health crisis that transformed global society and economies
details.details: The disease COVID-19, caused by the SARS-CoV-2 virus, was first reported in Wuhan, China, in December 2019. The World Health Organization declared a pandemic on 11 March 2020. Vaccines were first authorized in December 2020, and the WHO ended the global health emergency in May 2023.
details.culturalContext: Many countries used lockdowns, travel limits and mask rules, and remote work and schooling became widespread. The WHO recorded about 7 million reported deaths worldwide, excess-death estimates run higher, and the economic and social effects were large.

events.title: RUSSIA-UKRAINE WAR
events.description: Full-scale Russian invasion of Ukraine, often called the largest war in Europe since World War II

details.title: Russia-Ukraine War
details.description: Full-scale Russian invasion of Ukraine, often called the largest war in Europe since World War II
details.details: On 24 February 2022, Russia launched a full-scale invasion of Ukraine, eight years after it annexed Crimea and fighting began in the Donbas region. The conflict involved large ground forces, missiles and drones across Ukraine. Millions of Ukrainians fled the country.
details.culturalContext: The war led to wide sanctions on Russia, large military and financial aid to Ukraine from many countries, and changes in energy trade in Europe. Finland and Sweden applied to join NATO in 2022 and joined in 2023 and 2024.

events.title: ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE
events.description: Rapid advances in AI technology transform industries and raise new ethical questions

details.title: Artificial Intelligence
details.description: Rapid advances in AI technology transform industries and raise new ethical questions
details.details: In 2022 and 2023, tools such as ChatGPT (released November 2022) brought large language models to a wide public audience. They build on the Transformer architecture introduced in 2017 and on deep learning advances since the 2010s. Image and code generation tools spread alongside them.
details.culturalContext: AI systems began to be used in writing, programming, research and design, and raised questions about jobs, copyright, accuracy and safety. Governments began drafting rules, including the European Union AI Act, agreed in 2023 and in force from 2024.
